extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning to practise literary/poetry criticism (teachers of criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for close reading and the critical judgment of poems, emphasising how preconceptions distort reading and what substantive grounds a critic should attend to. Focuses on how to judge poetry beyond simplistic tests or doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical presuppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations about technical features (e.g. that rhymes must be perfect, that lines must not run over, that sonnets must have a definite division, that strict descriptive accuracy must be achieved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are usually accidental (from teaching or bad induction) rather than reasoned; while challengable, they often operate unreflectively. Test such presuppositions by asking whether the value-attribution they propose is directly serviceable in criticism, and be ready to abandon them if they blind you to what the poem actually does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-theory (value resides in subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that the value of a poem is simply the value of its subject (e.g. identifying a poem's subject and judging the poem good or bad because the subject is good or bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables quick but mistaken judgments (equating a faithful portrayal of a bad subject with a bad poem). Avoid evaluating a poem solely by whether its subject appeals to your taste; examine what the poem does with the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message-theory (value as inspirational message)
rubrics_metrics.description: The belief that a poem's worth lies in the presence of an 'inspiring message' or 'inspirational bit' which the reader finds or fails to find.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quest for message commonly determines reading and judgment but often blinds readers to other values. Recognise that inspirational content can be appropriate but is not a universal test of poetic worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lilt (musicality) as an independent test
rubrics_metrics.description: A preference for 'lilt' or musical flow taken as a standalone criterion of value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lilt is excellent where required by the poem, but as an independent demand it can render readers insusceptible to other, more important movements. Only accept lilt as a criterion when it accords with and is justified by the rest of the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-keyword doctrines (vivid, simple, musical, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that poetry must be characterized by a single definite quality (e.g. 'vivid', 'simple', 'musical', 'stirring', 'passionate', 'sensuous', 'impersonal', 'sincere').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such single-character keys are alluring but misleading: they encourage direct, simplistic application and ignore necessary alternatives, conditions, and qualifications. An adequate account of poetic value is intricate and resists straightforward application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of critical key-words
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical words like 'sincerity', 'truth', 'sentimentality', 'meaning', 'expression', 'form' carry many overlapping senses and are highly ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on these words as if univocal disguises vagueness and makes error likely. Disaggregate the possible senses in use before applying such terms; discover which 'missile' (sense) is relevant in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of doctrines converting choice into judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines attempt to convert an act of choice into an apparently safer activity of observation and application of rules—transforming choice into judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conversion tends to degrade genuine choice: judgment becomes a disguise that hampers the active choice required in criticism. Beware of substituting a poetic 'thermometer' (doctrine) for the critic's whole-minded decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited role of arguments and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments and principles can protect against irrelevancies, red herrings, and bad reasoning but cannot supply the ultimate reasons for liking or accepting a poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use principles to structure inquiry and guard against error (e.g. remind yourself of multiple aspects of a poem), but accept that at a crucial point a sheer choice may be necessary and arguments will not replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value rests on minute particulars and connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic value often depends on differences and connections so minute and unobtrusive that they cannot be directly perceived, yet are patent in their effects upon feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus attention on the poem's minute particulars and their effects; cultivate the capacity to detect subtle relations rather than expecting large, surface-level markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance as incorporation into the critic's fabric
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical act is essentially a choice about whether the new poem can be taken into the critic's whole personality/fabric of past experiences: 'Would the fabric afterwards be better or worse?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame judgment as whether acceptance would improve your 'fabric' (bearing in mind costs of reconstruction). Recognise internal conflicts and temporary provisional decisions; acceptance or rejection can involve personal change or minor obstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two ways preconceptions interfere
rubrics_metrics.description: Preconceptions interfere (1) by blinding the reader to other elements in the poem (forcing predilections on the poem), and (2) by blurring and disabling judgment (disguising vagueness as precision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for both effects: avoid forcing your preferred theory onto poems, and interrogate supposedly precise judgments that rest on ambiguous terms. Use experiments (e.g. protocols) to reveal the extent of such interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of preconception reduces direct applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The more refined and discriminating a preconception/theory is, the less possible it becomes to apply it directly as a test to a poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect complex accounts with many alternatives and qualifications; abandon the hope of a simple practical key. Use theoretical refinement to deepen understanding, not to produce a checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity as a special, complex criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is not a simple straightforward test; in a Confucian sense it can be a criterion of excellence when the discernment of what is good is made a matter of essential choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat sincerity as a multifaceted notion—sometimes useful as a negative indication, and occasionally as a principled standard when tied to whole-minded choice, but beware of its primitive unanalysed use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good reading requires whole-minded, decisive engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior critical judgment arises from penetrating 'far more whole-mindedly' into poetry and making it the occasion for decisive acts of the will rather than passive immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere acquiescent immersion in poetry (which can favour bad poems). Bring concentrated attention and the critic's full personality to bear when encountering a poem; this deliberate engagement is the 'secret of good judgment.'
